source.primary_manuscript: Library of Ashurbanipal Nineveh tablets (7th c. BCE; British Museum K series K.3375 + K.7752 + K.2252 + Sm. 4302 + others; recovered by Layard 1849)
source.primary_manuscript_dating: 7th c. BCE — Library of Ashurbanipal; the standard Babylonian recension compiled by Sin-leqi-unninni ~1200 BCE; the flood-narrative tradition extends to the early-2nd-millennium Atrahasis
source.primary_manuscript_contains: Tablet XI substantially complete; ~308 lines preserved
source.reference_critical_apparatus: George 2003 The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (Oxford, 2 vols) — the modern critical edition; Thompson 1930 The Epic of Gilgamish (Oxford, PD) — the public-domain critical edition; Smith 1873 The Chaldean Account of the Deluge (PD) — original discovery
source.transliteration_convention: Standard Assyriological convention per George 2003 + Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed. + Thompson 1930
source.verificationStatus: best-effort reconstruction; verification pending against George 2003 critical edition + original Nineveh codicology (BM K series). Transliteration is reconstructed from the published editions; sign-value reconstruction at the per-line level may contain errors but the sense-of-line is well-attested across editions.
source.fetchedFrom: Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed. (Bethesda) + George 2003 published portions + Thompson 1930 PD + ORACC corpus references
source.citation: George 2003; Thompson 1930; Smith 1873; Lambert-Millard 1969 Atra-Hasis; Tigay 1982 Evolution of Gilgamesh; Heidel 1949 Babylonian Genesis; Heidel 1946 Gilgamesh Epic and OT Parallels; Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed.; Kvanvig 2011 Primeval History
source.paleography_note: Tablet XI is well-preserved across the K-series Nineveh witnesses; minor lacunae and variant readings between K.3375 + K.7752 + Sm. tablets are documented in George 2003's apparatus. The line-numbering follows George 2003 (308 lines); Thompson 1930 differs slightly in line-numbering between the witness-collations.

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu-ma izakkara ana Ūta-napišti rūqi
notes: Opening line: 'Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant.' MAJOR THEME: the frame-dialogue of the entire flood-recitation begins. *rūqu* 'the Distant / the Faraway' — the standing epithet of Utnapishtim, the flood-survivor placed by the gods at *pî nārāti* 'the mouth of the rivers' (= the cosmic-boundary of the inhabited world).
'I gaze upon you, Utnapishtim.' Gilgamesh's incredulous opening: he expected a giant or a god, and finds an ordinary-looking man.

lines.translit: minâtu-ka ul šanâ kī yâši-ma atta
notes: 'Your features are not different — you are just like me.'

lines.translit: u atta ul šanâta kī yâši-ma atta
notes: 'And you yourself are not different — just like me you are.' Parallel-couplet emphasizing the human-likeness of the immortal Utnapishtim.
'(My) heart was fully ready to do combat (with you).' Gilgamesh confesses he had come prepared to fight.
'(But) you sit at your ease — idle.' Cross-corpus parallel to the trope of the deceptively-ordinary sage in wisdom-literature.

lines.translit: qibâ yâši kī tazziz-ma ina puḫur ilāni balāṭa teššēʾi
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Tell me — how is it that you stood in the assembly of the gods and sought (= obtained) life (= immortality)?' Gilgamesh's central question, which triggers the entire flood-narration. *balāṭa* 'life' here = immortality. Cross-corpus the Adapa-immortality-paradigm (adapa-woh): in Adapa, the *akāl balāṭi* 'food of life' is refused; in Gilgamesh, Utnapishtim has obtained the divine *balāṭu*. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the immortality-paradigm-question.

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti ana šâšu-ma izakkara ana Gilgāmeš
notes: 'Utnapishtim spoke to him — to Gilgamesh.' The narrative-baton passes; from here Utnapishtim narrates the flood in first person.

MAJOR THEME: 'Let me reveal to you, Gilgamesh, a hidden matter (*amāt niṣirti*).' The PROEM of the flood-narration. *amāt niṣirti* 'word of secret/treasure' — the disclosure-formula for a divinely-restricted teaching. Cross-corpus the Hebrew *sôd* / *sôd YHWH* (the divine council-secret); cross-corpus the Greek *mystērion*; cross-corpus the apocalyptic-revelation formulae (1 Enoch). LENS-RISK FLAG: 'hidden matter' is a magnet for esoteric / hidden-history readings; Editor: keep the philological frame, flag without endorsing.
'And the secret of the gods (*piriš-ti ilī*) I will tell you.' Doublet with v9. *pirištu* 'secret' is the standard Akkadian term for divine-restricted knowledge.
'Shuruppak — the city that you (yourself) know.' Shuruppak = modern Tell Fara; the antediluvian Sumerian city (cf. Sumerian King List). MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE.

lines.translit: ālu ša ina kišād Purattim šaknu
notes: 'The city that lies on the bank of the Euphrates (*Purattu*).' Geographic anchoring; the pre-flood Sumerian city is real-world locatable.
'That city was old (already) — and the gods (were) within it.' The antediluvian world: gods dwelling among humans.

lines.translit: ana šakāni a-bu-bi ub-lu libbi-šunu ilānu rabûtu
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'To make a flood (*abūbu*) — the great gods' hearts inclined.' THE DECISION-OF-THE-GODS line — the cosmic-decree that launches the flood. *abūbu* 'flood/deluge' is the standing Akkadian term; *ilānu rabûtu* 'the great gods' = the council. Cross-corpus the Sumerian Flood Story (flood-story-woh) Segment C — the gods' deliberation; cross-corpus Atrahasis Tablet II-III (Lambert-Millard 1969) — the noise-of-humanity rationale; cross-corpus Gen 6:5-7 the divine resolution to wipe out humanity. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE. LENS-RISK FLAG (Editor): popular Anunnaki-as-engineered-civilization readings cluster here; established WoH acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework — flag, do not theologize.
'Their father Anu took an oath with them (= bound them by oath).' Anu binds the council to the flood-decision by sworn oath; this is the cosmic-juridical step that locks the decree.
'Their counsellor, the warrior Enlil.' Enlil = the prime mover of the flood-decision (per Atrahasis tradition); the *malku* 'counsellor' as cabinet-figure.
'Their throne-bearer Ninurta.' Ninurta = the warrior-son of Enlil; here in his role as throne-bearer of the council.
'Their canal-inspector (*gugallu*) Ennugi.' Ennugi = the chthonic-canal-deity. MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *gugallu* 'canal-inspector / irrigation-officer' — the divine bureaucratic role.
'Prince Ea (*nin-šiku*) — with them was (party to) the oath.' Ea was part of the council and was bound by the oath of secrecy. This sets up the ethical-loophole that follows.

MAJOR THEME: 'Their (= the gods') word he (= Ea) repeated to the reed-hut (*kikkišu*).' THE EA-WARNING-FORMULA begins. The famous loophole: Ea is bound by oath not to tell humans, so he tells the reed-wall — and Utnapishtim, who happens to be on the other side, overhears. Cross-corpus the Sumerian Flood Story Segment D (Ziusudra at the wall); cross-corpus Atrahasis III i 19-23 (the reed-wall warning to Atrahasis). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the divine-warning-via-loophole motif.

'Reed-hut, reed-hut! Wall, wall!' The famous incantation-opening of Ea's address to the reed-wall. *kikkišu* and *igāru* are doubled in apostrophe. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the literally-most-quoted line of Tablet XI after the dove-and-raven.
'Reed-hut, hearken! Wall, pay heed!' Parallel to v21.
'O man of Shuruppak — son of Ubar-Tutu!' Utnapishtim's antediluvian patronymic. Ubar-Tutu = the last antediluvian king of Shuruppak per the Sumerian King List. MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE.

MAJOR THEME: 'Demolish the house — build a boat (*eleppu*)!' THE BOAT-CONSTRUCTION COMMAND. *eleppu* 'boat/ship' = the standard Akkadian term (cf. Sumerian *má*). Cross-corpus Gen 6:14 *tēbāh* (Heb. 'ark'); Qur'an 11:37 *al-fulk* (Arabic 'ship'); Sumerian Flood Story Segment E (Ziusudra's *má-gur8*). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.

'Abandon possessions — seek (after) life (*napšātu*)!' The famous renunciation-formula: trade material wealth for survival. *napšātu* (pl. of *napištu*) 'life' — the breath-life. Cross-corpus Matt 16:25 / Mark 8:35 'whoever would save his life will lose it' (DISAVOW as Christian-soteriological echo); cross-corpus Gen 12:1 (Abram leaves possessions for the journey).
'Cast off acquisitions — keep (your) life alive!' Doublet of v25; *bulluṭu* 'to keep alive' = D-stem of *balāṭu* (cross-link: the same root as Adapa's *akāl balāṭi*).

lines.translit: šūli-ma zēr napšāti kalāma ana libbi eleppi
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Bring up (= load aboard) the seed of all living things (*zēr napšāti kalāma*) into the boat.' THE ANIMAL-LOADING COMMAND. *zēr napšāti* 'seed of living-things' = the canonical Akkadian phrase. Cross-corpus Gen 6:19-20 (two of every living thing); Gen 7:2-3 (clean/unclean distinction); Qur'an 11:40 *min kullin zawjayn* 'of every (kind) a pair'; Sumerian Flood Story Segment E. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the animal-loading-canon.
'The boat that you will build…' Beginning of the boat-specifications.
'…let her dimensions be measured (precisely).' The precision-of-construction formula.

'Let her breadth and her length be equal.' THE CUBE-PROPORTION: the Babylonian flood-boat is built as a CUBE, not the rectangular ark of Genesis. Cross-corpus Gen 6:15 (300 × 50 × 30 cubits — a long boat-shape); Atrahasis III i 26-30 (square outline). MANDATORY: the boat-shape divergence between traditions.

'Like the apsû (the cosmic-freshwater-deep), make her roof.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *apsû* — the cosmic freshwater abyss, Ea's domain. The roofing-formula compares the boat to Ea's own cosmographic realm.

lines.translit: anāku idēma azakkara ana Ea bēlī-ya
notes: 'I (= Utnapishtim) understood, and I spoke to Ea my lord.' Utnapishtim begins his reply to Ea's instructions.
'The matter of my lord's speech — thus I have heeded.'
'I have understood; I shall (carry out the work). But what shall I answer (when asked)…?' Utnapishtim raises the practical problem: how to explain the boat-construction to his fellow-citizens.
'…(when) the city, the populace, and the elders (ask)?'
'Ea opened his mouth and spoke.' Standard speech-introduction formula.
'He said to me — to his servant.'
'You — thus shall you say to them:'

MAJOR THEME: 'Enlil has come to hate me…' THE FAMOUS DOUBLE-MEANING SPEECH begins. Ea coaches Utnapishtim in an equivocal address: literally it appears to say 'Enlil hates me, so I must leave town and go to Ea's-abyss', but in fact predicts the destruction of his neighbors. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.
'…I cannot dwell in your city.'

lines.translit: ina qaqqar Enlil ul ašakkana šēpī-ya
notes: 'On Enlil's earth I cannot set my foot.'

lines.translit: ur-rad-ma ana apsî it-ti Ea bēlī-ya ašab
notes: 'I shall descend to the apsû and dwell with Ea my lord.' The literal meaning suggests Utnapishtim is leaving town; the audience hears departure, but the gods hear the flood-secret.

MAJOR THEME: 'Upon you (= the people of Shuruppak) he (= Ea) will rain down abundance.' THE FAMOUS DOUBLE-ENTENDRE: *nuḫšu* 'abundance/fat-of-the-land' — but the same line continues with another rain-word that means destruction. The literal listener hears 'plenty'; the careful listener hears 'flood'. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE — the doubled-meaning of the omen.
'A bounty of birds, a secret-store of fishes.' The promised plenty — surface-meaning.
'[He will set] up a rich harvest.' The good-omen surface-meaning continues.

lines.translit: ina šēr kukkī ina līlâti ušaznan-kunūši šamûtū kibāti
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'In the morning he will rain down *kukkū* — in the evening he will rain upon you a rain of wheat (*kibātu*).' The famous DOUBLE-MEANING line: *kukkū* can mean 'darkness/cakes-of-darkness' (= disaster) or 'cakes' (= plenty); *kibātu* 'wheat' rhymes with *kibittu* 'heaviness/woe'. The omen reads as bounty to the unwary and as flood-disaster to the wise. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the equivocal-omen technique. Cross-corpus Greek oracle-doubletalk; cross-corpus Hebrew prophetic-ambiguity (e.g., Jonah 3:4 *nehpāket* 'will be overthrown OR will repent').
'As soon as morning brightened…' Beginning of the construction-execution sequence.

lines.translit: ina pī nāri pa-ḫi-ir mātu ana muḫḫi-ya
notes: '…at the mouth of the river the land gathered to me.' The community comes out to help build.
'The craftsman brought his axe.' First of the assembled-workforce.
'Strong men brought reed-mats / the carpenters their axes.' Tools and laborers assembled.
'The young carried the bitumen, the strong-armed brought what was needed.' Workforce description (Foster 2005).
MAJOR THEME: 'On the fifth day I laid down her hull/keel.' Begin: the 7-day construction-schedule (cf. Atrahasis-flood-week).
'Her floor (= base) was one *ikû* (= field-measure) — her sides one *kibru* each.' Dimensions: per George 2003 = each side ~120 cubits = ~60 m. The cubic-boat.
'Ten *nindan* each (= ~60 m) the height of her walls.' MANDATORY: confirms the cubic-shape (each dimension equal). Sumerogram NINDA.TA.ÀM = *nindan* unit, ~6 m each.
'Ten *nindan* each measured her sides.' Doublet for emphasis.
'I laid down her structure — I drew her design.'

MAJOR THEME: 'I gave her six decks (lit. roofed-her in six).' The SEVEN-DECK BOAT (counting hull + 6 deck-divisions; or 7 by some readings). Cross-corpus Gen 6:16 'with lower, second, and third decks' (Heb. *taḥtiyyîm šəniyyîm wə-šəlîšîm*) — but Hebrew has 3 decks vs. Babylonian 6/7. MANDATORY THEME: the multi-deck flood-boat tradition.
'I divided her into 7 (parts).' Doublet/clarification: seven internal compartments.
'Her interior I divided into 9 (sections).' Subdivision-of-the-decks for the cargo-of-living-things.

lines.translit: šigarī kīma ša mê amḫaṣ ina qabli-ša
notes: 'Water-plugs I drove into her middle (= bilge-plugs).' Practical shipwrightry.
'I made / saw to the punt-poles, the supplies.' Outfitting.

MAJOR THEME: 'I poured 3 *šār* (= ~3 × 3600 = 10,800 units) of bitumen (*kupru*, here *ESIR.UD.A*) into the kiln.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY: *kupru* 'bitumen / pitch'. Cross-corpus Gen 6:14 *kōper* 'pitch' (Heb. cognate of Akk. *kupru*); cross-corpus Qur'an 23:27 *al-tannūr* (the oven/kiln) and 11:38-39 the boat-construction. The PITCH-AND-BITUMEN TRADITION is a strong Hebrew/Babylonian cross-corpus link.
'I poured 3 *šār* of *ittû* (= asphalt) into her interior.'
'3 *šār* of (further) bitumen the basket-carriers brought up.' Massive quantities — the bitumen-treatment makes the boat watertight.

lines.translit: e-zib ŠÁR šamni ša anāku akula-ma
notes: 'Apart from the *šār* of oil that I myself ate (= consumed in the work)…' Additional supplies used in construction.
'…2 *šār* of oil the boatman stowed.' For sealing and for provisioning.
'For the workmen I slaughtered (lit. drowned/sank) oxen.' Feasting the workforce.
'I killed sheep daily.' The daily food-supply for the workforce.

lines.translit: šikara kurunna šamna karāna ana ummâni
notes: 'Beer, kurunnu-beer, oil, wine for the workmen…' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *šikaru* 'beer' (the staple Mesopotamian beverage); *kurunnu* (a fine quality beer-type); *karānu* 'wine'.
'…I let them drink as if (it were) river-water.' The simile-of-abundance — the workforce drinks plentifully.

'I held a festival as if it were the *akītu*-day.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *akītu* = the New Year festival, the highest cultic-celebration of the Babylonian year. The construction-feast is given New-Year-festival rank.
'I poured oil with my (own) hands.' Personal/ritual anointing.

MAJOR THEME: 'By [the] seventh day the boat was finished.' THE SEVEN-DAY CONSTRUCTION: the boat is built in 7 days. Cross-corpus the 7-day creation pattern (Gen 1); cross-corpus Atrahasis III i 38-39 (the 7-day construction); cross-corpus the Sumerian Flood Story 7-day flood (flood-story-woh). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the 7-day cosmic-marker.
'Her launch was difficult.' The boat is so large that launching is a struggle.
'They brought the launching-poles above and below.' Standard launching-procedure.
'(They moved her) until two-thirds of her had entered the water.' Launching-progress.
'Whatever I had I loaded her.' The lading-formula.
'Whatever I had of silver I loaded.'
'Whatever I had of gold I loaded.'

lines.translit: mim-ma īšû zēr napšāti kalāma uštēli ana libbi-ša
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Whatever I had of the seed of all living things I brought up into her.' THE LOADING-OF-LIVING-THINGS: parallels v27 — the canonical animal-loading-formula. Cross-corpus Gen 6:19 'two of every kind of living thing' (Heb. *mi-kol ḥay*). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.

lines.translit: uštēli ana libbi eleppi kala kimti-ya u salāti-ya
notes: 'I brought up into the boat all my family and kin (*kimtu* + *salātu*).'

lines.translit: būl ṣēri umām ṣēri mārī ummâni kalī-šunu uštēli
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'The cattle of the field, the wild beasts of the field, all the craftsmen — I brought up.' THE CRAFTSMEN-LOADING is unique to the Mesopotamian tradition (the Genesis ark has only Noah's family, no craftsmen). MANDATORY: a key divergence from the Hebrew tradition — Utnapishtim saves the *ummânū* (craftsmen) too, preserving the antediluvian technical-knowledge.
'Shamash had set an appointed-time (*adannu*).' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *adannu* 'the fixed time' — the divinely-decreed deadline. Shamash here is the time-keeping deity.

lines.translit: ina šēr kukkī ina līlâti ušaznana šamûtū kibāti
notes: 'In the morning *kukkū* — in the evening a rain of wheat (will fall).' Repetition of the double-meaning omen of v46 — now as fulfillment-trigger.

lines.translit: erub ana libbi eleppi-ma pe-ḫi bāb-ki
notes: 'Enter the boat — and seal your door!' The PILOTING-COMMAND.
'That appointed-time arrived.'

lines.translit: ina šēr kukkī ina līlâti uš-az-na-an šamûtū kibāti
notes: 'In the morning *kukkū* — in the evening rained the rain of wheat.' Triple-repetition (vv46, 84, 87) marks the omen-fulfillment moment.
'I watched the (changing) face of the day-weather.'
'The day for omen-watching looked ominous.'

lines.translit: pa-la-ḫa-an-ni-ma ana libbi eleppi e-ru-ub-ma e-te-di-il bābī
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'I was afraid — I entered the boat and sealed my doors!' THE SEALING-OF-THE-ARK. Cross-corpus Gen 7:16 'YHWH shut him in' (Heb. *wa-yyisgōr YHWH baʿadô*) — but in Genesis YHWH closes the door; in Tablet XI Utnapishtim closes it himself. NOTABLE DIVERGENCE.
'For the sealing of the boat…'

MAJOR THEME: '…to Puzur-Amurri the boatman.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *Puzur-Amurri* — the named boatman/pilot. Theophoric: 'Secret-of-Amurru'. Cross-corpus the named-boatman tradition (cf. Sumerian Flood Story; Atrahasis has a similar figure).
'I handed over (= gifted) the palace with its goods (to him).' Utnapishtim rewards the pilot.
MAJOR THEME: 'As soon as morning brightened…' THE FLOOD-DAWN: the morning of the deluge breaks.

lines.translit: i-lam-ma iš-tu i-šid šamê ur-pa-tu ṣa-lim-tum
notes: MAJOR THEME: '…from the horizon of heaven there rose up a black cloud (*urpatu ṣalimtu*).' THE FAMOUS BLACK-CLOUD line — opening of the flood-itself. *ṣalmu* 'black' (cf. Heb *ṣelem* 'image' — false cognate). Cross-corpus Gen 7:11 'all the springs of the great deep burst forth and the floodgates of heaven were opened'.

MAJOR THEME: 'Adad in its midst was thundering.' THE STORM-GOD MANIFESTS. *Adad* = the storm-god (cf. Hadad in West-Semitic; Baal-Hadad in Ugaritic; the YHWH-as-storm-god typology in early Hebrew poetry, Ps 29). MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE.

lines.translit: Šullat u Ḫaniš illakū ina maḫri
notes: 'Shullat and Hanish go in advance (= as heralds).' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: Shullat and Hanish = the twin-storm-heralds (the bull-vanguard of Adad). The cosmic-procession-of-the-storm.
'The throne-bearers (= divine ushers) go (forth) over mountain and land.'

MAJOR THEME: 'Errakal tore out the mooring-poles.' Errakal = a Nergal-aspect (death/pestilence god); the *tarkullū* 'mooring-poles' that hold the cosmos in place are ripped up — cosmic-de-mooring. STRONG IMAGE.
'Ninurta went, the (dyke-)dams he caused to overflow.' Ninurta-as-irrigation-warrior breaks open the cosmic dykes.

MAJOR THEME: 'The Anunnaki raised their torches.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *Anunnaki* — the chthonic council-of-gods (often the Anunnakū = the underworld-gods as opposed to the Igigi = the heavenly-gods, though usage varies). LENS-RISK FLAG (Editor): the Anunnaki are the magnet-term for popular-fringe ET-civilization readings (Sitchin etc.); WoH established acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework — flag, do not theologize. The torches = the lightning-flashes illuminating the storm.
'With their bright-radiance they set the land ablaze.' The lightning-image continues.
'Adad's stupor (*šuḫarratu* = paralyzing-terror) passed over the heavens.'
'Whatever was bright he turned to darkness.' Cosmological-inversion: the storm makes day into night.
'The land (was) shattered like a pot.' Famous simile of cosmic-fragility.
MAJOR THEME: 'For one day the storm-wind blew.' Begin: the flood-duration count.
'Swift it blew — to the mountains it (came/destroyed). The deluge!'

lines.translit: ki-ma qabli eli nišī i-ba-aʾ kašūšu
notes: 'Like a battle the cataclysm came upon the people.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *kašūšu* 'cataclysm/disaster-weapon' — a divinely-wielded annihilation-instrument.
'Brother could not see brother (his brother).' The blinding-darkness-formula.
'People could not be recognized from the sky (= from above).'

MAJOR THEME: 'The gods (themselves) became afraid of the flood.' THE FAMOUS GODS-IN-FEAR LINE. STRONG IMAGE: the flood is so destructive that even the gods who decreed it are terrified. Cross-corpus the Sumerian Flood Story Segment F (the gods weep); cross-corpus Atrahasis III ii. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.

lines.translit: it-ḫi-šum-ma i-te-lu-ú ana šamê ša Anim
notes: MAJOR THEME: '(They) shrank back, they fled up to the heaven of Anu.' THE GODS' FLIGHT UPWARD.

lines.translit: ilānu ki-ma kalbi kun-nu-nu ina kamāti rab-ṣu
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'The gods, like dogs, were curled up — they cowered outside (at the wall).' THE FAMOUS GODS-CURLED-LIKE-DOGS simile. Theologically humbling: the gods reduced to fearful animals. STRONG LITERARY CANDIDATE. Cross-corpus the Sumerian Flood Story (gods cower); Foster 2005's signature-line of the tablet.
'Ishtar cried out like a woman in childbirth (*ālittu*).' Famous simile of cosmic-anguish.

lines.translit: ú-na-am-ba bēltu ša ilī ṭābat rigma
notes: 'The lady of the gods, sweet of voice, wailed.' Ishtar's lament continues.

lines.translit: ūmu ulli-tu ana ṭiṭṭi lū i-tu-ur-ma
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'That former day (= the old world) — let it (have) turned to clay (*ṭīṭu*)!' Ishtar's lament: 'would that the previous-time had crumbled to clay'. *ṭīṭu* 'clay' (cross-corpus Gen 2:7 *ʿāpār* 'dust' / Atrahasis 'clay-of-the-apsû' as the substance of human creation).

lines.translit: aššu anāku ina puḫur ilāni aqbû lemnêti
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Because I (= Ishtar) myself spoke evil in the assembly of the gods.' ISHTAR'S CONFESSION OF COMPLICITY. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: divine-self-incrimination.

lines.translit: ki-i aqbû ina puḫur ilāni lemnêti
notes: 'How could I have spoken evil in the assembly of the gods…!' Doublet for emphasis.
'I commanded a battle to destroy my (own) people.' Ishtar as the mother-of-humanity admits she voted for the flood.
'I myself bore (gave birth to) my (own) people.'
'Like spawn of fishes they fill the sea!' Bitter image: the drowned humans fill the waters like fish-fry.
'The Anunnaki-gods wept with her.'
'The gods sat in mourning.'
'Their lips were covered — were parched.' Image of divine-grief.

MAJOR THEME: 'For six days and seven nights…' THE FAMOUS FLOOD-DURATION (Babylonian tradition). Cross-corpus Gen 7:12 (Heb. 40 days + 40 nights — divergent count); cross-corpus Atrahasis (7 days); cross-corpus the Sumerian Flood Story (7 days + 7 nights, flood-story-woh). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the flood-duration tradition. NOTABLE DIVERGENCE Gen-vs-Babylonian: 40 vs. 7.

lines.translit: il-lak šāru abūbu mēḫû i-sa-pan māta
notes: '…the wind blew — the flood-deluge — the storm-wind levelled the land.'

lines.translit: ina 7-šu kašād(i) ūmi i-nu-uḫ abūbu mēḫû qabla
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'When the seventh day arrived, the flood-deluge — the storm — the war (= cataclysm) — abated.' THE STILLING-OF-THE-STORM moment.
'(The storm) which had battled like a woman in labour…' Returns to the simile of v114.
MAJOR THEME: 'The sea grew quiet, became silent.' THE WATERS-CALM moment.
'The evil-wind, the flood ceased.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *imḫullu* 'evil-wind' — the destructive cosmic-wind (cf. Enuma Elish IV).
'I looked out at the day — its sound was stilled.'

lines.translit: u kullat tenēšeti i-tu-ra ana ṭiṭṭi
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'And all of humanity had returned to clay (*ṭīṭu*).' THE ENTIRETY-OF-HUMANITY-TO-CLAY moment. *tenēšētu* 'humanity' (cf. Hebrew *ʾenôš* — phonological-resonance but the Akkadian is from *teneš* root). Cross-corpus Gen 7:21-23 'all flesh perished'; Gen 3:19 'to dust you shall return'. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.
'(The flood-plain) was flat like a roof.' Image of total flattening.

lines.translit: ap-te nappišta-ma ṣētu ūmma im-ta-qut eli dūr appī-ya
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'I opened a vent — and daylight fell on the side of my nose (= my cheeks).' THE OPENING-OF-THE-HATCH moment. The cosmic-claustrophobia released. STRONG IMAGE.

lines.translit: uš-qam-ma-ma ki-mi-iṣ-ya eli appī-ya il-li-ku dīm-tum
notes: 'I bent down — I sat down — I wept. Over my nose the tears flowed.' THE FAMOUS TEARS-OF-UTNAPISHTIM moment.
'I looked out across the world-quarters — (the world had become) the edge of the sea.'
'At a distance of 12 (units) a region rose.' First sighting of land.

MAJOR THEME: 'On Mount Nimuš the boat came to rest.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: KUR Nimuš (Mount Nimuš), older reading 'Mount Niṣir'. Cross-corpus Gen 8:4 *hārê Ararat* 'mountains of Ararat' — NOTABLE DIVERGENCE (Babylonian Nimuš in the Zagros vs. Hebrew Ararat in Armenia); cross-corpus Qur'an 11:44 *al-Jūdī* (Mt Judi, in modern SE Turkey/northern Iraq — close to the Babylonian Nimuš). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the mountain-landing tradition.

lines.translit: šadû Nimuš eleppa iṣbat-ma a-na nâši ul iddin
notes: 'Mount Nimuš held the boat fast — gave (it) not to move.'
'One day, two days, Mount Nimuš held (the boat).'
'Three days, four days, Mount Nimuš held (the boat).'

lines.translit: 5 ūma 6 ūmī šadû Nimuš iṣbat-ma ana nâši ul iddin
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Five days, six days, Mount Nimuš held the boat fast.' Standard 7-day cosmic-marker leading to the bird-test.
MAJOR THEME: 'When the seventh day arrived…'

MAJOR THEME: 'I brought out a dove (*summatu*) and released (it).' THE BIRD-TEST BEGINS — the dove. MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *summatu* 'dove'. Cross-corpus Gen 8:8-12 'and he sent out a dove' (Heb. *yônāh*); cross-corpus the Sumerian Flood Story (no surviving bird-test); cross-corpus the Berossus version (which preserves a bird-test). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the BIRD-TEST tradition.
'The dove went, came (back).'
'(There was) no resting-place — and she returned.'

MAJOR THEME: 'I brought out a swallow (*sinuntu*) and released (it).' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *sinuntu* 'swallow' — the SECOND BIRD. NOTABLE DIVERGENCE from Genesis (Gen has dove-dove-dove sequence; Babylonian has dove-swallow-raven).
'The swallow went, came (back).'
'(There was) no resting-place — and she returned.'

MAJOR THEME: 'I brought out a raven (*āribu*) and released (it).' THE THIRD BIRD — the raven (*āribu*). Cross-corpus Gen 8:7 (the raven, which goes back and forth and does not return); Gen sends raven FIRST then dove — INVERSE-ORDER compared to Babylonian (Babylonian: dove → swallow → raven; Hebrew: raven → dove → dove → dove).
'The raven went, the receding waters it saw…'
MAJOR THEME: '…it ate, it foraged, it cawed (?), it did NOT return.' The raven finds dry land. STRONG MOMENT: the survival-confirmation.

MAJOR THEME: 'I brought (everything) out — I made an offering to the four winds.' THE DISEMBARKATION + SACRIFICE. Cross-corpus Gen 8:20 (Noah builds an altar and offers burnt-sacrifice); cross-corpus the post-flood-sacrifice tradition. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.

lines.translit: aš-kun sur-qe-nu eli zikkurati ša šadî
notes: 'I set up an incense-offering upon the ziggurat of the mountain (-peak).' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *surqennu* 'incense-offering' / 'flour-offering'; *ziqqurratu* 'ziggurat / stepped-tower' — here applied to a mountain-peak as natural-temple.

MAJOR THEME: 'Seven and seven cult-vessels (*adagurru*) I set up.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *adagurru* — a clay cult-vessel for libations. The fourteen-vessel formula. Cross-corpus the sacred-seven-and-seven Hebrew tradition (Gen 7:2 seven pairs of clean animals).

lines.translit: ina šap-li-šu-nu at-bu-uk qanâ ereni u asu
notes: 'Beneath them I poured out (= burned) reed, cedar, and myrtle.' The aromatic-incense formula. *erenu* 'cedar' (cross-corpus the Hebrew *erez* — Phoenician cedar of Lebanon).

MAJOR THEME: 'The gods smelled the fragrance (*erīšu*).' THE FAMOUS PLEASING-FRAGRANCE moment. Cross-corpus Gen 8:21 'YHWH smelled the pleasing aroma (*rêaḥ ha-niḥōaḥ*)' — DIRECT PARALLEL, both at Heb. and at semantic level. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the pleasing-fragrance tradition.
'The gods smelled the sweet fragrance.' Cross-corpus Gen 8:21 *rêaḥ ha-niḥōaḥ* exactly. ALMOST WORD-FOR-WORD parallel.

lines.translit: ilānu kīma zumbī eli bēl niqê ip-taḫ-ru
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'The gods gathered like flies (*zumbū*) around the sacrificer (*bēl niqê*).' THE FAMOUS GODS-LIKE-FLIES simile. Theologically loaded: the post-flood gods are FAMISHED — they have had no sacrifices during the flood, and now swarm to the smoke. The reduction-of-divinity to insect-greed. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE; also: Atrahasis III v 30-35 has the same image. Heidel 1946 highlights this as the most theologically-significant divergence from Gen — where YHWH alone smells the savor, here the gods are reduced to flies. CRITICAL CROSS-CORPUS DIVERGENCE FLAG.

lines.translit: iš-tu ul-la-nu-um-ma bēltu rabītu ina kašādi-ša
notes: 'From of old, when the great lady (= Ishtar / Belet-ili) was arriving…' The narrative-shift to Ishtar's complaint.

lines.translit: ul-li nimēqī rabûti ša Anum īpu-šu kī ṣubāti-ya
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'She lifted up the great lapis-lazuli (necklace) which Anu had made for me as a (love-)token.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: the *nimēqī rabûtu* = Ishtar's great lapis-lazuli necklace (an iconic divine-jewelry). Cross-corpus Gen 9:13 'I have set my bow (= rainbow) in the cloud' — NOTABLE PARALLEL: a colorful-arc-shaped divine-object set in heaven as a post-flood covenantal-sign. The Babylonian rainbow = Ishtar's necklace.

lines.translit: ilānu annūti lū lapis-uknī ina kišādī-ya lū la amaš-ši
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'These (lapis-lazuli) jewels at my neck — let me never forget (them).' Ishtar swears by her necklace to remember the flood. Cross-corpus Gen 9:14-16 (the rainbow as YHWH's memorial of the no-second-flood covenant). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the RAINBOW-MEMORIAL tradition.

lines.translit: ūmī annûti lū aḫsus-su ana dāri lū la amaš-ši
notes: 'These days I will remember — never to be forgotten.' Doublet of v162.
'Let the gods come to the incense-offering.'
MAJOR THEME: 'But let NOT Enlil come to the incense-offering!' Ishtar's CURSE/BAN of Enlil from the sacrifice. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: divine-excommunication.
'Because — without taking counsel — he caused the flood.' Ishtar's INDICTMENT: Enlil decreed unilaterally.
'And consigned my (own) people to destruction.'
MAJOR THEME: 'As soon as Enlil arrived…' Beginning of the ENLIL-CONFRONTATION.
'…he saw the boat — and Enlil flew into a fury.'

MAJOR THEME: 'He was filled with rage against the Igigi-gods.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *Igigi* — the seven (or ten) great gods of heaven (contrast Anunnaki = chthonic gods). LENS-RISK FLAG: like Anunnaki, Igigi is a fringe-popular term.
'Has anyone come out alive?'
'Let no man have survived the destruction!'
'Ninurta the warrior answered and spoke.'
'…to the warrior Enlil.'

lines.translit: man-nu-um-ma ša lā Ea i-ban-na-a a-ma-ta
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Who but Ea could (have) devise(d) the matter?' Ninurta indicts Ea as the leak.
'And Ea — he knows every (sort of) craft.'
'Ea the warrior answered and spoke.'
'…to the warrior Enlil.'
MAJOR THEME: 'You — wise-sage of the gods, warrior!' Ea begins the FAMOUS EA-DEFENSE / WISDOM-AND-PROPORTION speech.

lines.translit: ki-i ki-i lā tam-tal-lik-ma a-bu-ba taš-kun
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'How — how could you, without (taking) counsel, have caused a flood?!' Ea's INDICTMENT of Enlil's unilateral act.

MAJOR THEME: 'Lay the sin on the sinner (*bēl ḫīṭīti*) — lay the offense on the offender (*ḫīṭu*).' THE FAMOUS INDIVIDUAL-vs-COLLECTIVE JUSTICE PRINCIPLE — Ea's proportionality speech. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the personal-responsibility principle. Cross-corpus Ezek 18:20 (Heb. 'the soul that sins shall die'); cross-corpus Deut 24:16 ('parents not put to death for children'). NOTABLE: this is one of the earliest extant divine-justice-as-proportionate articulations in ancient Near Eastern literature.
'Lay the trespass (*gillatu*) on the trespasser.' Doublet of v181.
'Loosen (= relent) — that he be not cut off; pull (back) — that he be not unsettled.'

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba nēšu lit-bā-ma nišī liṣaḫḫir
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Instead of (your) sending a flood, let the LION arise and diminish the people.' Ea proposes a PROPORTIONAL alternative-punishment: the lion-cull instead of total annihilation. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba barbara lit-bā-ma nišī liṣaḫḫir
notes: 'Instead of (your) sending a flood, let the WOLF arise and diminish the people.' Parallel-line.

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba ḫušaḫḫu liššakin-ma māta li-iš-[gi-iš]
notes: 'Instead of (your) sending a flood, let FAMINE (*ḫušaḫḫu*) be established and lay waste the land.' Cross-corpus Atrahasis II i-iv (Atrahasis cycles through drought + famine + plague-attempts before the flood-decision).

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba dErra lit-bā-ma māta liš-giš
notes: 'Instead of (your) sending a flood, let ERRA (= plague-god) arise and lay waste the land.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: Erra = the plague-god (cf. Erra Epic). Cross-corpus the four-horsemen tradition (Rev 6) of war + famine + pestilence + death — disavow Christian-soteriological pre-resolution but flag the typological-pattern.

lines.translit: anāku ul ap-ta-a piriš-ti ilī rabûti
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'I (= Ea) did not (myself) reveal the secret of the great gods.' THE FAMOUS EA-DENIAL of having directly revealed the secret. The technical loophole: Ea spoke to the reed-wall, not to a human.

lines.translit: atra-ḫasīs šunatti ušabri-šum-ma piriš-ti ilī iš-me
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'To Atra-ḫasīs (= Utnapishtim) — I caused a dream to appear, and the secret of the gods he (himself) heard (from it).' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *Atra-ḫasīs* (lit. 'Surpassingly Wise') — the SECOND NAME of Utnapishtim, drawn directly from the Atrahasis tradition. Cross-corpus the Akkadian Atrahasis epic (Lambert-Millard 1969). Ea claims he delivered the warning via DREAM, not via direct speech — a further legal-technical loophole.
'Now, then — take counsel for (Utnapishtim)!'
MAJOR THEME: 'Enlil went up into the boat.' THE RELENT-AND-RECONCILIATION moment.
'He took me by my hand — he brought me up to the deck.'
'He brought up — he made my wife sit beside me (= as my equal).' The dignifying-of-the-wife act.

lines.translit: u-lap-pit putta-ni i-zi-iz ina bi-ri-ni i-ka-ar-ra-ban-na-ši
notes: 'He touched our foreheads, stood between us, and blessed us.' The ROYAL-BLESSING gesture (touching the forehead = formal divine-conferment).
MAJOR THEME: 'In times past, Utnapishtim was (only) human (*amēlūtu*).'

lines.translit: i-na-an-na Ūta-napišti u sinništu-šu lū e-mu-u kī ilāni nâši
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Now Utnapishtim and his wife shall become like us — the gods!' THE FAMOUS DEIFICATION line: Utnapishtim and his wife are RAISED TO DIVINE STATUS. Cross-corpus Gen 3:22 'the human has become like one of us' (the divine recognition-of-godlike-status) — but in Gen this is the cause of expulsion; in Gilgamesh it is the REWARD. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the DEIFICATION-OF-THE-FLOOD-SURVIVOR. Cross-corpus the Adapa-loss-of-immortality contrast (adapa-woh) — Adapa refuses divine food and stays mortal; Utnapishtim is given divinity outright. KEY PAIRING.

lines.translit: lū-ši-ib Ūta-napišti ina rūqi ina pī nārāti
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Let Utnapishtim dwell far away, at the mouth of the rivers (*pī nārāti*).' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *pī nārāti* 'mouth of the rivers' — the COSMIC PERIPHERY where the deified Utnapishtim is settled. Cross-corpus the Hebrew Eden-as-river-source (Gen 2:10-14, four rivers); cross-corpus the Greek Hesperides + the islands-of-the-blest. The far-edge-of-the-world placement of the immortal.

lines.translit: il-qu-šu-in-ni-ma ina rūqi ina pī nārāti uš-bu-ʾi-in-ni
notes: 'They took me — at the mouth of the rivers, in the distance, they settled me.'

lines.translit: i-nu-ma ka-a-ša mannu ana ka-a-ša ilāni upaḫḫar-ma
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'And now — as for you (= Gilgamesh) — who will gather the gods for your sake…' UTNAPISHTIM'S FRAME-CONCLUSION: he turns the narrative back on Gilgamesh. The flood-and-deification was a one-time event; you, Gilgamesh, cannot expect the same. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the immortality-is-not-repeatable principle.
MAJOR THEME: '…that you may find the (eternal) life which you seek?' The CENTRAL QUESTION re-stated.

lines.translit: alka — 6 ūmī u 7 mušâti la taṣallal
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Come — for six days and seven nights do not sleep!' THE FAMOUS SLEEP-TEST. The narrative-conclusion: Utnapishtim challenges Gilgamesh to a humanly-impossible task as a precondition for immortality. The seven-night marker mirrors the flood-duration. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.
'But as he sat upon the threshold (*paršu*)…'
MAJOR THEME: '…sleep like mist enveloped him.' Gilgamesh fails the test immediately. STRONG IMAGE.

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti izakkara ana šâši ana sinništi-šu
notes: 'Utnapishtim spoke to her — to his wife.'
'Behold the young man who sought (eternal) life!'
'Sleep like mist enveloped him.'

lines.translit: sinništu izakkara ana šâšu ana Ūta-napišti rūqi
notes: 'The (wife) spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant.'
'Touch him — let the man wake!'

lines.translit: ḫarrāna ša illika lū ina šal-mim li-tu-ra
notes: 'Let the road he came (by) return him in peace.'

lines.translit: [ina] bāb ša u-ṣu-u li-tu-ra ana māti-šu
notes: 'By the gate from which he went out, let him return to his land.'

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti izakkara ana šâši ana sinništi-šu
notes: 'Utnapishtim spoke to her — to his wife.'
MAJOR THEME: 'Always humanity (*amēlūtu*) deceives — it will deceive you (too).' Utnapishtim's CYNICAL REPLY: humans claim what they cannot deliver; Gilgamesh will deny he slept.

lines.translit: alki epi-šu-ma akala u šukni eli muḫḫi-šu
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Come — bake bread (*akalu*) and set (it) by his head!' THE SEVEN-LOAVES TEST. Each day's loaf will register the passage of time.

lines.translit: u ūmī ša iṣ-ṣa-lu-lu ina igāri ušan-ni
notes: 'And the days that he slept — on the wall (*igāru*) mark them.'
'She baked his loaves — and set (them) by his head.'

lines.translit: u ūmī ša iṣ-ṣa-lu-lu ina igāri uš-ta-an-ni-šu
notes: 'And the days that he slept on the wall she marked.'
MAJOR THEME: 'His first loaf was (already) dried out.' Begin the SEVEN-LOAVES catalogue: each loaf's state of decay measures the days slept.
'The second — leathery. The third — soggy.'
'The fourth — its crust had turned white.'
'The fifth — had cast (a) mould.'
'The sixth — (still freshly) baked.'
'The seventh — (still) on its coals — (just then) he touched him (= Utnapishtim woke Gilgamesh).' The seven-loaves catalogue completes at the moment of awakening.
'The man woke up.'

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ūta-napišti rūqi
notes: 'Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant.'
MAJOR THEME: 'Just (now) as I was about to fall asleep — you touched me…!' Gilgamesh's FAMOUS DENIAL: he claims he only just dozed off. Confirms Utnapishtim's prediction in v212.
'Swiftly you touched me — and you wakened me!'
'Utnapishtim [spoke to him] — to Gilgamesh.'
'Come, Gilgamesh — count your loaves!'

lines.translit: u ūmī ša ta-aṣ-lu-lu lu-u i-du-šu-uš-ka
notes: 'And the days you slept — let them be known to you!'
'Your first loaf was dried out.' (Repetition of the catalogue, now told to Gilgamesh.)
'The second leathery, the third soggy.'
'The fourth — its crust turned white.'
'The fifth — cast mould.'
'The sixth — (freshly) baked.'

lines.translit: se-bu-u ina pi-in-ti-šu i-na pa-na-tu-uš-šu-ma lap-tat-ka
notes: 'The seventh — on its coals — and (just then) I touched you.' The seven-loaves verdict is delivered to Gilgamesh.

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ūta-napišti rūqi
notes: 'Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant.'
MAJOR THEME: 'What shall I do, Utnapishtim — where shall I go?' GILGAMESH'S DESPAIR: his failure is exposed.
'A snatcher (*ekkimu* = demon/ghoul) has seized my flesh.'
MAJOR THEME: 'In my bed-chamber Death dwells.' Cross-corpus the Hebrew motif of death-in-the-house (Job 17:13).
'And wherever I set my foot — there too is Death!'

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti izakkara ana šâšu ana Ur-Šanabi malāḫi
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Utnapishtim spoke to him — to Ur-Shanabi the boatman.' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: Ur-Shanabi = Utnapishtim's ferryman who brought Gilgamesh across the Waters of Death.
'Ur-Shanabi — may the harbor reject you, the crossing-place avoid you!' (Utnapishtim curses Ur-Shanabi for ferrying a mortal across.)

lines.translit: ša ina aḫi-šu it-tal-la-ku zummâta aḫa-šu
notes: 'You who walked along its (= the death-shore's) bank — forsake (now) that bank.'

lines.translit: amēlu ša tu-ub-la-an-na šuʾattim ina pā-ni-ka
notes: 'The man whom you brought — his body is shameful before you (= unwashed/unkempt).'
'(Cause that) the skin be washed pure (that) the bloom of his (handsome) figure (return to him).'
'Let his garment be cast off — (let it) be clean.'
'Let (him) — may the sea-waters bear (it) away (from him).'
'Let his body be made sound (= cleansed) — let his head be made pure.'

lines.translit: kar-bal-la-tu lu na-aš-šat ki-li-il-ši lu-tar-ri ana ṣē-ri-šu
notes: 'Let him put on a new turban — let the wraparound (=robe) be restored to his back.'
'Until he goes to his (own) city.'
'Until he travels his road.'

lines.translit: kar-bal-la-tu ay i-tar-ru-uš kib-ba-šu lū eššâ-ma
notes: 'The turban let it not be removed — let it be ever-new (= maintained).'
'Ur-Shanabi took him — made him sit at the wash-basin (*mutullû*).'

lines.translit: ma-aš-ka i-ki-šum-ma ina mê tâmtim it-bal
notes: 'He washed his skin — the waters of the sea bore (the filth) away.'
'(So) was the body made pure — his head cleansed.'
'The garment of (old) skin was cast off — and the sea bore it away.'
'He put on the new turban — his wraparound was new.'

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš u Ur-Šanabi i-tab-ka-nim-ma ina eleppi ir-ka-bū
notes: 'Gilgamesh and Ur-Shanabi (now) embarked — they sailed away in the boat.' THE DEPARTURE.
'They set the boat (loose) — they crossed over (the waters).'

lines.translit: sinništu-šu ana šâšu ana Ūta-napišti rūqi
notes: MAJOR THEME: '(His) wife (spoke) to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant.' Begin: the WIFE'S INTERVENTION for the parting-gift.
'Gilgamesh came — he toiled — he laboured.'
MAJOR THEME: 'What will you give him — that he may return to his land?'
'And he, Gilgamesh, lifted up the punt-pole.'
'He drove the boat toward the shore.'

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti ana šâšu izakkara ana Gilgāmeš
notes: 'Utnapishtim spoke to him — to Gilgamesh.'
'Gilgamesh, you came, you toiled, you laboured.'
MAJOR THEME: 'What can I give you that you may return to your land?' THE PARTING-GIFT QUESTION.
MAJOR THEME: 'Let me reveal to you, Gilgamesh, a hidden matter (*amāt niṣirti*) — '. Mirroring v9 — Utnapishtim now reveals a SECOND secret: the plant of rejuvenation.

lines.translit: u piriš-ti ša ilāni kâ-ša luqbî-ka
notes: 'And the secret of the gods (*pirištu*) — I will tell you.'

MAJOR THEME: 'There is a plant (*šammu*) — its appearance is like the boxthorn (*eddetu*).' MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *šammu* 'plant/herb' (here = the plant of rejuvenation); *eddetu* 'boxthorn' (a spiny plant). Cross-corpus Gen 2:9 (the tree of life in Eden); Gen 3:22 (the tree of life as antidote to mortality); Qur'an 20:120 (the 'Tree of Immortality' that the Devil shows Adam). STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the PLANT-OF-IMMORTALITY tradition.
'Its thorns (are) like the brier-bush — they (will) prick your hand.'
'If your hands can obtain that plant…'
MAJOR THEME: '…you (will) find your (renewed) life.' The PLANT-OF-REJUVENATION promise: not immortality, but rejuvenation.
'When Gilgamesh heard this…'

lines.translit: ip-tu-ú raṭ-ṭam(?) ina šēpē-šu it-mu-uḫ abnē kabtūti
notes: 'He opened a channel(?) — at his feet he tied heavy stones.'
MAJOR THEME: 'They drew him down (= the stones pulled him down) into the apsû.' THE DIVING-TO-RETRIEVE-THE-PLANT moment. Gilgamesh dives by weighted-descent into the freshwater-abyss.
'He himself grasped the plant — (and) it pricked his hand.'
'He cut (loose) the heavy stones beneath him.'
'The sea bore him up — to its shore.'

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ur-Šanabi malāḫi
notes: 'Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Ur-Shanabi the boatman.'
MAJOR THEME: 'Ur-Shanabi — this plant is a plant of (anxious-)pulsating (= rejuvenation).' STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the plant's purpose announced.
MAJOR THEME: '(The plant) by which a man finds his (renewed) life-breath.'

MAJOR THEME: 'To Uruk-of-the-sheepfold I will carry it!' Gilgamesh's plan: bring rejuvenation to Uruk. MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *Uruk supūri* 'Uruk the sheepfold' — the canonical epithet of Uruk.

MAJOR THEME: 'I will feed (it) to an elder — let him test its (effects).' The PROOF-BY-OLD-MAN-TRIAL — share the plant communally. The renunciation-of-personal-immortality gesture (or: cautious-empirical attitude).
'Its name shall be: (See!) The Old Man is Made Young!' MAJOR THEME: the plant's name is announced. STRONG IMAGE: 'The Old-Man-Becomes-Young (Again).'

lines.translit: anāku-ma lūkulam-ma lu-tu-ra ana šib-bu-ut su-uḫ-ri-ya
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'I myself shall eat (it) — and return to (the days of) my youth!' The self-administered version of the plant's promise. The MID-LIFE-RENEWAL hope.
'At twenty leagues they broke off a piece (= took a meal).'
'At thirty leagues they made a camp.'

lines.translit: ī-mur Gilgāmeš būrtam-ma ša mē-ša kaṣû
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Gilgamesh saw a pool — its water was cool.' THE FATEFUL-BATHING moment begins.
'He went down into it — he bathed in the water.'

MAJOR THEME: 'A serpent (*ṣēru*) smelled the fragrance of the plant.' THE FAMOUS SERPENT-STEALS-IMMORTALITY moment. MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: *ṣēru* 'serpent'. Cross-corpus Gen 3:1-7 (*nāḥāš* the serpent of Eden) — the SAME REPTILE in a DIVERGENT etiology: in Gen the serpent introduces death to humanity by tempting Eve to eat; in Gilgamesh the serpent steals the immortality-plant directly. CRITICAL CROSS-CORPUS PARALLEL: the serpent-and-immortality theme. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE. Also: Qur'an 20:117-121 (Iblis-as-tempter of Adam re: immortality). Note that the serpent's immortality-via-shedding (next line) supplies a folkloric etiology for snake-sloughing.
MAJOR THEME: 'From [the depths(?)] it (= the serpent) emerged — it carried away the plant.' THE THEFT.
MAJOR THEME: 'In going back — it shed (its) skin.' THE FAMOUS SERPENT-SLOUGHING ETIOLOGY: the snake's annual skin-shedding is its rejuvenation, stolen from humanity. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.
MAJOR THEME: 'On that day Gilgamesh sat down and wept.' THE WEEPING moment — the loss of the plant.
'Down the side of his nose his tears flowed.'
'He spoke to Ur-Shanabi the boatman.'
MAJOR THEME: 'For whom, Ur-Shanabi, did my arms grow weary?'
'For whom has the blood of my heart been spent?'
MAJOR THEME: 'I gained no good for myself.' The FAMOUS LAMENT-OF-FUTILITY.

MAJOR THEME: 'For the lion of the earth (= the serpent) I have done the good (deed)!' BITTER IRONY: the serpent benefited from Gilgamesh's labor. The reading 'lion of the earth' = *nēš erṣetim*, an epithet of the serpent (cf. George 2003).
'Now — at twenty leagues — the tide (already) bears (it) away.'

lines.translit: ina pe-ti-ya raṭ-ṭu(?) e-zib u-na-tī ina elippi
notes: 'In my opening (the channel?) I have left my tools in the boat.'
'At twenty leagues they broke off a piece (= took a meal).'
'At thirty leagues they made a camp.'
MAJOR THEME: 'When they reached Uruk-of-the-sheepfold…' THE RETURN-TO-URUK moment.

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ur-Šanabi malāḫi
notes: 'Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Ur-Shanabi the boatman.'

lines.translit: e-li-ma Ur-Šanabi ina muḫḫi dūri ša Uruk i-tal-lak
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Go up, Ur-Shanabi — walk upon the wall of Uruk!' THE FAMOUS CLOSING: Gilgamesh's wisdom-acquisition = he has come to see the WALL HE HAS BUILT as his real immortality. The legacy-in-stone substitution for personal-immortality. Cross-corpus Eccl 1-2 (the futility-and-legacy meditation); cross-corpus the entire ancient-near-eastern *šumu* 'name/fame' tradition. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE: the closing line that ties Tablet XI back to Tablet I's opening (the wall of Uruk).

lines.translit: te-me-en-na ḫi-iṭ libitta ṣub-bi šum-ma libnat-su lā agurri u uš-šu-šu lā id-du ru sebet mu-un-ta-li-ki
notes: MAJOR THEME: 'Inspect the foundation — examine the brickwork! (See) — is not its brickwork (made) of baked-brick (*agurru*)? And did not the SEVEN SAGES (*muntalkū* = the Seven Wise-Ones, the *apkallū*) lay its foundations?' THE FINAL LINE — closing-formula matching the opening of Tablet I (which begins with the same wall-inspection). MANDATORY GLOSSARY CANDIDATE: the SEVEN SAGES (*apkallū* / *muntalku*) = the antediluvian sage-bringers-of-civilization; cross-corpus the *apkallū* tradition (Berossus, Bīt mēseri); cross-corpus the Sumerian *abgal* tradition; cross-corpus Prov 9:1 'Wisdom built her house, hewed her seven pillars' (Heb. *šivʿāh ʿammûdêhā*); cross-corpus the seven-sages-of-Greece motif. LENS-RISK FLAG: the *apkallū* are the second magnet-term (after Anunnaki) for fringe-popular ET-civilization-bringers-of-knowledge readings; WoH acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework. STRONG CENTRAL CANDIDATE.
